title: Strands Decider Automation: Is It Worth It? (2026)
summary: Strands decider automation routes requests to agents or people based on rules. Understand setup, operational limits, and troubleshooting for issues.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces fits around a Strands agent


Before the agent and after it, Activepieces does the work: starting the run when a business event happens, and handling approval and notifications once the decider has answered.


It has 750 integrations to start those runs from and send those notifications through, and it doesn't configure Strands or replace the routing step itself.


Because of the Activepieces split, your 20 tests stay meaningful: the part you test stays small and the plumbing around it stays visible.


### The workflow on the canvas


Here is the shape on the canvas below: a new HubSpot lead starts the flow, an AI Agent step qualifies it, a condition checks the answer, and the branches add the lead to Salesforce, post to Slack, or send a Gmail follow-up.


Take from it that the decision is one box among seven, and every box before and after it is an ordinary step you can read.


### Triggering an agent run from a business event


Before the decider has done any work, each event you wire up spends credits, because the trigger is where a ticket or lead becomes an agent run.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) '[pricing guide](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/activepieces-cloud-pricing-plans-2026-price-guide) lists 1,000 credits a month on Free, 10,000 on Plus and 50,000 on Team.


At 300 tickets a day, a support queue is about 9,000 a month, so **Free runs out in the first few days** . Plus is the lowest tier with room for even one step per ticket.


Count steps, not tickets: a flow with an agent step, a condition and two notifications costs more per event than the trigger alone.


Point the trigger at the same input the 20 tests use. If a real angry email routes differently from your test copy, you want to see that in the run history, not in a customer's reply.


### Human approval after a decision


Put a person between the decider's answer and any action that is hard to undo, such as a refund, an account lock or a message to an executive. A wrong escalation costs more than a slow one.


To pause the flow until someone approves or rejects, Activepieces has a human approval step, and a rejection becomes a log entry you can use to fix the routing list.


Every plan, including free, allows unlimited flows, so a separate approval flow for each risky action doesn't use up a flow allowance.


Don't bother with any of this if your agents only run from a script you start yourself. Skip it as well if volume sits well under 1,000 runs a month and nobody needs notifying, so basic tooling won't become your bottleneck.


A plain function call around the Strands agent is simpler and has less to break.
